questions.question: The Expert Group Report on Comprehensive Updation of the CPI identified a data-quality problem with the existing CPI's rural sampling frame. What was the problem, and what did the Expert Group recommend?
options: The rural sampling frame was based on an outdated Census (2001) despite rapid urbanization since then, so the Expert Group recommended drawing a fresh sample of villages from the more current rural sampling frame used in the 2022-23 Household Consumption Expenditure Survey (HCES)
The rural sampling frame covered too many villages, so the Expert Group recommended cutting the number of villages sampled by half
There was no rural sampling frame at all prior to this Expert Group's recommendations
The Expert Group recommended abandoning rural CPI compilation altogether due to frame problems
questions.explanation: The report notes that the CPI's existing rural sampling frame relied on the 2001 Census, which had grown outdated given rapid urbanization and demographic change in the intervening two decades, risking a frame that no longer represented the current distribution of villages and their populations well. The Expert Group therefore recommended drawing a fresh sample of villages using the more current rural sampling frame that had been developed for the 2022-23 Household Consumption Expenditure Survey. It did not recommend halving the village count, and a rural frame did already exist (just an outdated one) -- and abandoning rural compilation was never proposed.

questions.locator: Expert Group Report on CPI, index-formula recommendations (Jevons index properties)
questions.source_excerpt: 7. Preserved Jevons Properties: Retains geometric mean benefits, limits outlier... In view of the above advantages, EG recommended to adopt the Jevons short (chain-linked) index.
questions.question: The Expert Group Report on CPI recommended adopting the Jevons index formula (a geometric-mean-based elementary aggregate formula) partly because of its favourable behaviour with respect to outlier price quotations. Why does a geometric-mean-based formula like Jevons tend to be less sensitive to outliers than a simple arithmetic mean of price relatives?
options: Because the geometric mean discards the largest and smallest price relatives before averaging, exactly like a trimmed mean

Because the geometric mean multiplies price relatives together and takes an n-th root, which dampens the influence of an extreme price relative compared to an arithmetic mean, which adds price relatives directly and lets one extreme value pull the whole average proportionally
Because the geometric mean can only be computed when all price relatives are exactly equal to each other
Because the geometric mean is mathematically identical to the arithmetic mean for any set of numbers
questions.explanation: The geometric mean of a set of price relatives is the n-th root of their product, which compresses the effect of any single very large or very small relative far more than an arithmetic mean does, since the arithmetic mean is a simple additive average where one outlier's magnitude directly shifts the sum (and hence the average) in proportion to its size. This outlier-dampening property, along with other desirable index-number properties the geometric mean satisfies, is exactly why the Expert Group favoured the Jevons formula for elementary aggregation. It does not work by discarding extreme values like a trimmed mean (option A), it does not require equal price relatives (option C), and geometric and arithmetic means are mathematically distinct except in the trivial case where all values are identical (ruling out option D).

questions.locator: Expert Group Report on CPI, weighting diagram recommendations
questions.source_excerpt: it was recommended that the expenditure on ganja be re-distributed among other items of the... series, no longer holds. Accordingly, it was recommended that all weighted items (358)...
questions.question: The Expert Group Report on CPI recommended redistributing the expenditure weight of an item like 'ganja' (which is illegal to sell and hence cannot be legally price-quoted) to other items in the basket. What data-quality principle does this kind of weight redistribution address?
options: It ensures that the total weighting diagram still sums to 100% even when a specific item can no longer be legitimately priced or tracked, by spreading its share proportionately across related, trackable items
It is done purely to reduce the total number of items in the basket, with no bearing on weight totals
It increases the overall inflation rate reported by the CPI series
It has no effect on the internal consistency of the weighting diagram
questions.explanation: A CPI weighting diagram's item weights must sum to 100% (or to the total expenditure share of the relevant group) for the index to be internally consistent. When an item cannot legitimately be priced or tracked -- as with an illegal item like ganja, for which no legal retail price quotation is possible -- its allocated expenditure weight has to be redistributed (typically pro-rata) among the remaining, trackable items in the same category, so that the overall weighting diagram remains complete and consistent rather than silently losing weight. This is a data-quality and index-integrity fix, not a mechanism to change the reported inflation rate directly (option C) or simply to shrink the item count (option B); the redistribution has everything to do with maintaining internal consistency, contrary to option D.

Since, the base year to account for seasonal variations and price volatility in certain commodities...
questions.question: According to the Expert Group Report on CPI, what is one key criterion for selecting a good 'base year' for a CPI series?
options: The base year should be as far in the past as possible, to maximize the length of the resulting time series

The base year should be as close as possible to (ideally overlapping with) the weight-reference year, and should be a normal, representative year without unusual seasonal or price volatility distorting it
The base year should always be a leap year, for ease of monthly calculations
The base year should be chosen randomly to avoid any selection bias by statisticians
questions.explanation: The report reiterates the well-established CPI compilation principle that the base year -- the reference period against which subsequent index values are measured -- should be as close as possible to (ideally the same as) the year from which the expenditure weights (the weighting diagram) were derived, so that the base-period prices and the base-period weights refer to a consistent point in time. It should also be a 'normal' year, free from atypical price volatility, supply disruptions, or seasonal distortions that could bias the whole series measured relative to it. There is no requirement that it be a leap year, chosen at random, or as far in the past as possible; in fact, an outdated base year is exactly the kind of data-quality problem CPI updation exercises are meant to correct.

questions.locator: NQAF-CoCSSO presentation, Quality indicators slide
questions.source_excerpt: Quality indicators for a statistical product can describe a product in terms of relevance, accuracy and reliability, timeliness and punctuality, coherence and comparability, accessibility, clarity etc.
questions.question: Per MoSPI's NQAF-CoCSSO assessment presentation, which set of dimensions is used to describe the quality of a statistical output product?
options: Cost, staffing, and office location
Relevance, accuracy and reliability, timeliness and punctuality, accessibility and clarity, and coherence and comparability
Political sensitivity, media coverage, and public opinion polling results
The number of employees involved in producing the statistic
questions.explanation: The presentation lists the standard set of quality dimensions used to describe a statistical output: relevance (whether it meets user needs), accuracy and reliability (how closely it reflects the true value), timeliness and punctuality (how quickly and predictably it is released), accessibility and clarity (how easily users can obtain and understand it), and coherence and comparability (whether it is consistent internally, over time, and with other sources). These are the internationally recognized quality dimensions used across national quality assurance frameworks including the UN NQAF; production cost, staffing levels, political sensitivity, and headcount are operational or contextual factors, not the quality dimensions themselves.

questions.locator: NQAF-CoCSSO presentation, Assessment methodology slide
questions.source_excerpt: Checklist to review lines of the NQAF: Checklist to assess the system/ product by marking 'yes', 'no', 'partially true' or 'not applicable'.
questions.question: How did MoSPI assess the Indian Statistical System against the UN's National Quality Assurance Framework (NQAF), in terms of the scoring method used?
options: By assigning a single overall numerical score out of 100 to the entire statistical system with no element-level detail

By using a checklist that marks each individual quality element as 'Yes', 'No', 'Partially true', or 'Not applicable', and then aggregating these across the 19 quality statements and their underlying elements
By outsourcing the entire assessment to an international audit firm with no involvement of MoSPI staff
By surveying ordinary citizens about their trust in government statistics
questions.explanation: The NQAF-CoCSSO checklist methodology works at a granular level: each of the many quality elements underlying the 19 NQAF quality statements is individually marked as 'Yes' (fully met), 'No' (not met), 'Partially true' (partially met), or 'Not applicable', and these element-level marks are then aggregated (with 'Partially true' counted as half weight, per the assessment's own scoring convention) into category-level and overall percentages. This granular checklist approach, not a single opaque overall score, a purely external audit, or a general public-opinion survey, is what let the assessment identify specific gaps (such as the absence of a legislative framework for the NSO) rather than just a headline number.

questions.locator: NQAF-CoCSSO presentation, Non-response errors slide
questions.source_excerpt: measuring enumerator bias using interpenetrating sub-sampling, followed in NSSO surveys is useful. However, re-interviewing is not done due to constraints.
questions.question: The NQAF-CoCSSO presentation describes 'interpenetrating sub-sampling', as followed in NSSO surveys, as a technique used for what specific purpose?
options: To increase the total sample size of a survey without additional cost

To measure enumerator bias, by splitting the sample so that different enumerators independently cover comparable, interpenetrating sub-samples of the same target population, allowing systematic differences between enumerators' results to be detected
To replace face-to-face interviews entirely with telephone interviews
To determine the optimal number of strata for a stratified sample
questions.explanation: Interpenetrating sub-sampling divides an overall sample into two or more sub-samples that are each independently representative of (interpenetrate) the same target population, and assigns different enumerators or teams to each sub-sample under otherwise identical conditions. Because each sub-sample should, in principle, yield similar estimates if there were no enumerator effects, any systematic difference in results between the sub-samples/enumerators reveals enumerator bias or variability -- a non-sampling error source that is otherwise very hard to detect and quantify. This is fundamentally a design for isolating and measuring interviewer effects, not a way to cheaply inflate sample size, a substitute for face-to-face interviewing, or a stratification-count optimization technique.

questions.locator: NQAF-CoCSSO presentation, Data Quality and Statistical Disclosure Control slide
questions.source_excerpt: As per NQAF, access to microdata is allowed for research purposes, subject to specific rules and protocols on statistical confidentiality that are made known publicly and posted on the agency's website. ...Dissemination of unit level data by deleting / suppressing identification particulars of respondents to protect their privacy and confidentiality.
questions.question: Per the NQAF-CoCSSO presentation, how does the Indian Statistical System balance making microdata (unit-level data) available for research against protecting respondent confidentiality?
options: Microdata is never released to any external researcher under any circumstances, to guarantee zero disclosure risk

Microdata is released for research purposes, but with identification particulars deleted or suppressed, and access is governed by confidentiality rules and protocols that are made public and posted on the agency's website
Microdata is released only to foreign governments and never to domestic researchers
Respondent names and addresses are always published alongside the data to ensure full transparency
questions.explanation: The NQAF-aligned approach described allows access to unit-level microdata for legitimate research purposes, but only after direct identification particulars of respondents are deleted or suppressed, and subject to documented confidentiality rules and protocols that are made publicly known (e.g., posted on the agency's website), so that both researchers and the public understand the conditions under which such access is granted. The presentation also acknowledges that indirect identification of respondents may still be possible even after this de-identification, which is why restricted-data procedures and further transformation of data are sometimes needed. This is a middle path, not a blanket denial (option A), a foreign-only policy (option C), or the opposite extreme of publishing identifying details openly (option D).

questions.locator: SIF Guideline v1.1, Objective, para 1
questions.source_excerpt: The objective of these guidelines is to facilitate and assist State Governments in the development of a State Level Monitoring Framework including institutional arrangements to track the progress on the SDGs by building on the existing National Indicator Framework.
questions.question: What is the stated objective of MoSPI's 'SIF Guideline, version 1.1' document?
options: To directly compile and publish the State Indicator Framework on behalf of every State Government
To assist and guide State Governments in developing their own State-level SDG monitoring framework and institutional arrangements, building on the existing National Indicator Framework (NIF)
To replace the National Indicator Framework entirely with a single unified state-level framework
To rank all States and Union Territories by their overall economic performance
questions.explanation: The SIF (State Indicator Framework) Guideline explicitly states its purpose is to facilitate and assist State Governments -- not to do the work for them -- in developing their own State Level Monitoring Framework for tracking SDG progress, including the institutional arrangements needed to sustain it, using the existing National Indicator Framework as the foundation to build upon. It is guidance for States to adapt and extend the NIF according to their own local priorities and data realities, not a replacement of the NIF, a MoSPI-authored compilation done on the states' behalf, or a general economic-performance ranking exercise (which is closer to what NITI Aayog's separate SDG Index does).

questions.locator: SIF Guideline v1.1, para 16, Guiding Principle: participatory development
questions.source_excerpt: 16. SIF is to be prepared in a participatory manner: The development of the State Indicator Framework is expected to follow a process with the involvement / consultation of all stake holders and ownership with the State. Bypassing the consultative process or a non-involved outsourcing of its development to a consultant will reduce the likelihood of its successful implementation.
questions.question: The SIF Guideline warns against one particular approach to developing a State Indicator Framework, saying it 'will reduce the likelihood of its successful implementation'. What is that approach?
options: Involving too many government departments in the consultation process
Bypassing the consultative process with stakeholders, or fully outsourcing the framework's development to an external consultant without State involvement
Using digital tools and dashboards to visualize the indicators
Aligning the State framework too closely with the National Indicator Framework
questions.explanation: The Guideline's first stated principle is that the SIF must be developed participatorily, with genuine consultation of stakeholders and ownership retained by the State government itself; it explicitly warns that either bypassing this consultative process, or handing off the framework's development to an external consultant without the State's own involvement, undermines the likelihood that the resulting framework will actually be implemented successfully, since local buy-in and institutional ownership are treated as essential to sustained use of the framework. Over-involving departments, using digital dashboards, or aligning closely with the NIF are not identified as risks in the Guideline -- indeed, alignment with the NIF is separately encouraged as a different guiding principle.

questions.locator: General concept area of this UPSC Statistics paper's syllabus: operating characteristic curve in acceptance sampling
questions.source_excerpt: This UPSC Statistics (Main) paper's syllabus covers statistical quality control, including the Operating Characteristic (OC) curve of a single sampling plan; grounded in that well-established syllabus area rather than a specific transcribed question.
questions.question: In acceptance sampling for quality control, the Operating Characteristic (OC) curve of a sampling plan plots which relationship?
options: The cost of inspection against the sample size used

The probability of accepting a lot against the lot's true (actual) fraction defective, showing how well the plan discriminates between good and bad lots across the full range of possible quality levels
The number of defective units found against the time taken to inspect the lot
The producer's profit against the consumer's satisfaction rating
questions.explanation: The OC curve is the defining performance summary of a single (or multiple) sampling plan: for every possible true fraction defective p that an incoming lot might actually have, it plots the probability that the plan would accept that lot, Pa(p). A steeply falling OC curve (dropping quickly from near-1 acceptance probability at low p to near-0 acceptance probability at high p) indicates a plan that discriminates sharply between good and bad lots, while a shallow curve indicates poor discrimination. This is exactly the tool used to read off the producer's risk (probability of rejecting a genuinely good lot at the AQL) and the consumer's risk (probability of accepting a genuinely bad lot at the LTPD) that a given (n, c) sampling plan delivers. It has nothing to do with inspection cost versus sample size, defect counts versus time, or profit versus satisfaction.

questions.locator: General concept area of this UPSC Statistics paper's syllabus: control charts and process control
questions.source_excerpt: This UPSC Statistics (Main) paper's syllabus covers statistical process control, including the distinction between chance (common) causes and assignable (special) causes of variation on a control chart; grounded in that well-established syllabus area rather than a specific transcribed question.
questions.question: In statistical process control, a process is said to be 'in a state of statistical control' when the variation observed on its control chart is attributable to which type of cause?
options: Only assignable (special) causes, such as a specific machine malfunction or a change of raw material batch

Only chance (common) causes -- the many small, inherent sources of random variation always present in a stable process -- with no identifiable assignable causes producing points outside the control limits or non-random patterns
A process is 'in control' only when there is exactly zero variation in the measured quality characteristic
A process is 'in control' whenever the sample size used for each subgroup exceeds 30
questions.explanation: A process is considered to be in a state of statistical control when the only variation present is due to chance (common) causes -- the numerous small, inherent, and individually unidentifiable sources of variability that are always present in any process, producing points that stay within the control limits and show no systematic non-random pattern. The presence of an assignable (special) cause, such as a tool breaking, a new operator, or a raw-material change, typically produces an out-of-control signal (a point beyond the control limits, or a non-random run or trend), which is precisely what a control chart is designed to detect and flag for investigation. Zero variation is neither expected nor required for a process to be 'in control' (option C is wrong), and being in control has nothing to do with a fixed subgroup sample size threshold like 30 (option D).

questions.locator: Manual on Consumer Price Index 2010, Chapter III, para 3.42, Selection of Base Year
questions.source_excerpt: 3.42 The well known criteria for the selection of base year are:- (i) a normal year i.e. a year in which there is no...
questions.question: Per MoSPI/CSO's Manual on Consumer Price Index 2010, what is one of the well-known criteria the manual lists for selecting the base year of a Consumer Price Index series?
options: The base year should be a 'normal' year -- one without abnormal fluctuations, shortages, or other unusual conditions that would distort prices
The base year must always be exactly 50 years before the current year
The base year should always fall on a leap year
The base year should be the year in which the CPI series is first published, regardless of price conditions that year
questions.explanation: The Manual sets out standard, internationally recognized criteria for base-year selection, foremost among them that the base year should be a 'normal' year, meaning one free of abnormal conditions such as unusual shortages, extreme price shocks, natural disasters, or other atypical events that would make prices in that year unrepresentative of typical conditions. Using such a distorted year as the reference point would bias every subsequent index value computed relative to it. There is no such requirement that the base year be exactly 50 years in the past, a leap year, or the same year the series happens to be first published (in practice, revisions typically use expenditure survey years as the source of the weighting diagram, and the base year is chosen to align closely with that).

questions.question: Per the Manual on Consumer Price Index 2010, most Consumer Price Index series across the world, including India's, are compiled using which index formula, and why?
options: The Fisher Ideal index, because it is the simplest formula to compute with limited data

The Laspeyres' formula, mainly because of its practical simplicity, since it uses fixed base-period quantities/weights so that only current prices need to be collected each period, not current quantities
The Paasche's formula, because it most accurately tracks real-time changes in consumption patterns
A simple unweighted arithmetic mean of all prices, with no use of expenditure weights at all
questions.explanation: The Manual explains that CPI series worldwide predominantly use the Laspeyres' formula, which is a base-weighted average of price relatives: it fixes the quantities (or, equivalently, the expenditure weights) at their base-period values, so that compiling the index in any later period only requires collecting current prices, not current quantities, which would require a fresh expenditure survey every period. This practical simplicity is precisely why Laspeyres dominates in practice despite its known upward bias over time relative to a true cost-of-living index, whereas the Paasche formula requires current-period quantities and is therefore 'seldom used in practice' per the Manual, and the Fisher Ideal index (a geometric mean of Laspeyres and Paasche) requires both, making it even more data-intensive, not simpler.

questions.locator: Manual on Consumer Price Index 2010, Chapter III, paras 3.14-3.16
questions.source_excerpt: 3.14 In normal economic situations, the Laspeyres' index shows an upward bias (in relation to the true cost of living index) with the passage of time while the Paasche's index shows a... ideal index as the geometric mean of the Laspeyres' and Paasche's indices...
questions.question: Per the CPI Manual 2010, the Laspeyres index tends to show an upward bias relative to a true cost-of-living index as time passes, while the Paasche index tends to show a downward bias. What underlying consumer behaviour explains this pair of biases?
options: Consumers tend to substitute away from goods that have become relatively more expensive towards goods that have become relatively cheaper, a behaviour that Laspeyres (using old, base-period quantities) fails to capture, while Paasche (using current quantities that already reflect this substitution) tends to over-correct for it
Prices generally fall over time for all goods, so any fixed-weight index is automatically biased upward
Consumers buy exactly the same basket of goods every period with no substitution at all, making both formulas equally biased in the same direction
The bias exists purely due to rounding errors in the calculation, unrelated to any real economic behaviour
questions.explanation: The Laspeyres/Paasche bias pattern is a textbook consequence of consumer substitution behaviour: as relative prices change, rational consumers substitute towards goods that have become relatively cheaper and away from those that have become relatively more expensive. Laspeyres, by holding quantities fixed at base-period levels, ignores this substitution and so overstates the true cost of maintaining the base-period standard of living (an upward, or 'substitution', bias). Paasche, by using current-period quantities that already reflect this substitution response, tends to understate the cost of maintaining the base standard of living relative to a true cost-of-living index (a downward bias). This is precisely why the geometric mean of the two (the Fisher Ideal index) is often treated as a closer approximation to the 'ideal' index. The bias is a real economic phenomenon tied to substitution, not a rounding artifact, and it does not require the false premise that all prices fall over time or that consumption baskets never change.

questions.locator: Manual on Consumer Price Index 2010, Chapter III, paras 3.16, 3.42 (weighting diagram revision interval)
questions.source_excerpt: revision of weighting diagrams of Consumer Price Index series 'at intervals not more than 10 years'... the weighting diagram is built up at the start of the series usually on the basis of a [Family Living/Consumer Expenditure] Survey...
questions.question: According to the Manual on Consumer Price Index 2010, the weighting diagram of a CPI series is built at the start of the series from a household expenditure survey, and is meant to be revised at what maximum interval?
options: Every month, alongside the regular price collection
At intervals not more than 10 years
Only once, at the launch of the series, and never revised again for as long as the series continues
Every 50 years, in line with each decennial Census cycle rounded to the nearest half-century
questions.explanation: The Manual specifies that the weighting diagram -- the set of expenditure-share weights derived from a household budget/consumer expenditure survey that determines how much influence each item has on the overall index -- should be revised at intervals not exceeding 10 years, so that the weights continue to reflect a reasonably current pattern of household consumption rather than becoming progressively outdated as spending habits shift. Monthly revision (option A) would defeat the purpose of having a fixed weighting diagram between revisions, never revising at all (option C) would let the weights become badly outdated exactly as the Expert Group Report later found had happened, and a 50-year interval (option D) is far longer than the Manual's stated maximum.

questions.locator: Manual on Consumer Price Index 2010, Chapter III, para 3.16
questions.source_excerpt: 3.16 There are two essential constituents of a CPI namely, (i) the weighting diagram and (ii) retail prices.
questions.question: Per the Manual on Consumer Price Index 2010, what are the two essential constituents needed to compile a Consumer Price Index?
options: GDP growth data and interest rate data
The weighting diagram (expenditure weights for each item) and retail prices (collected regularly for those items)
Import and export trade statistics
Population Census totals and literacy rates
questions.explanation: The Manual identifies the weighting diagram (the relative expenditure shares of different items/groups, established from a household consumption expenditure survey) and retail prices (the actual price quotations collected periodically for those same items from designated markets/outlets) as the two essential building blocks of any CPI. Without the weighting diagram, there would be no basis for combining individual item price movements into a single overall index number reflecting how households actually spend; without regularly collected retail prices, there would be nothing to plug into that weighting structure each period. GDP data, trade statistics, and Census literacy figures play no direct role in CPI compilation itself.

questions.locator: National Accounts Statistics: Sources and Methods 2012, Chapter 1, paras on periodic base-year revision
questions.source_excerpt: Over the years, the base years of NAS series have also undergone changes... the base year of national accounts series is changed [periodically]... as base year (hereafter referred to as...) primarily because in the base year...
questions.question: The National Accounts Statistics: Sources and Methods, 2012 document describes a long history of the CSO periodically revising the base year of India's National Accounts series (e.g., 1948-49, then successively later years). Why does a national accounts base year need periodic revision at all?
options: Because the mathematical formula for computing GDP changes every time the base year changes

Because as the structure of the economy evolves over time -- new industries emerge, consumption and production patterns shift, and new data sources become available -- an outdated base year and its associated weighting/classification structure no longer reflect the current economy well, so periodic rebasing keeps the accounts representative
Because the Constitution of India requires a base-year change with every new Five-Year Plan
Because the base year must always coincide with a national election year
questions.explanation: The document's own account of the successive base-year revisions (1948-49 through to 2011-12 and beyond) is a direct response to structural change in the Indian economy: as new economic activities emerge, old ones shrink in relative importance, survey methodologies improve, and new administrative/survey data sources become available, a base year and its associated commodity/industry classification and weighting structure that was current when adopted gradually becomes outdated and less representative of the present-day economy. Periodic rebasing exercises incorporate updated data sources, revised classifications, and current weighting patterns to keep the national accounts estimates methodologically sound and representative. There is no constitutional mandate tying base-year changes to Five-Year Plans or elections, and the core GDP estimation formulas (production, income, expenditure approaches) do not themselves change with each rebasing, only the underlying data and weights do.

questions.source_excerpt: GVA per worker from... round (2005-06). The GVA per worker from... arrive at the GVA per worker estimate for... expenditure incurred on cultivation of... GVA estimates have been compiled by... a product of GVAPW of 63rd round of NSSO
questions.question: For segments of the economy where direct enterprise-level output data is scarce (such as parts of the unorganised sector), the National Accounts Statistics: Sources and Methods, 2012 describes estimating Gross Value Added (GVA) as the product of which two quantities?
options: The average GVA per worker (GVAPW), typically derived from an NSSO survey round, multiplied by an estimate of the total workforce engaged in that segment
The number of registered companies multiplied by their average paid-up capital
The total government budget allocation for that sector multiplied by an inflation adjustment factor
The population of the state multiplied by its literacy rate
questions.explanation: Where comprehensive enterprise-level output or income data is not directly available -- typically for unorganised-sector and some private-sector activities -- the National Accounts methodology estimates GVA indirectly as the product of an average GVA-per-worker (GVAPW) figure, usually benchmarked from a specific NSSO employment-unemployment or enterprise survey round (such as the 63rd round referenced in the document), and a workforce estimate for that segment (how many workers are engaged in the activity, from Census or NSSO employment data). This 'workforce approach' substitutes for direct output measurement precisely because unorganised-sector units are too numerous and informal to survey comprehensively every year. Budget allocations, paid-up capital of registered companies, and population/literacy figures are not the inputs to this specific GVAPW-based estimation method.

questions.question: Per the National Accounts Statistics: Sources and Methods, 2012 document, one of the successive revisions of India's national accounts base year moved the series to which base year, as described in the document's historical account?
options: 1948-49, the very first base year the CSO ever used
2004-05, one of the later base-year revisions the document traces in its historical account
2050-51, a future-dated base year
1776, the year of a foreign country's political founding, used only for international comparability
questions.explanation: The document traces the successive base-year revisions of India's National Accounts Statistics from the CSO's original 1948-49 base year through several later revisions, one of which moved the series to a 2004-05 base year, as part of the periodic rebasing exercise the document describes. A base year of 1948-49 was the historically first base year, not the one this later revision moved to; a future-dated year (2050-51) makes no sense for a base year describing historical estimates; and 1776 is an unrelated foreign historical date irrelevant to India's national accounts.

questions.locator: National Accounts Statistics: Sources and Methods 2012, standard GDP estimation framework
questions.source_excerpt: GVA of former is measured through the commodity flow... expenditure approach. The broad... or less same as the one used in 1999-00...
questions.question: National accounts practice, as reflected in the CSO's National Accounts Statistics: Sources and Methods, recognizes three standard, conceptually equivalent approaches to estimating a country's aggregate economic output (GDP/GVA). What are these three approaches?
options: The production (output) approach, the income approach, and the expenditure approach
The urban approach, the rural approach, and the combined approach
The import approach, the export approach, and the trade-balance approach
The public-sector approach, the private-sector approach, and the household approach
questions.explanation: National accounting recognizes that a country's aggregate output can, in principle, be measured three equivalent ways: the production (or output) approach, which sums the value added by each industry/sector after netting out intermediate consumption from gross output; the income approach, which sums all factor incomes generated in production (compensation of employees, operating surplus, mixed income, taxes less subsidies on production); and the expenditure approach, which sums final expenditures on goods and services (consumption, investment, government spending, and net exports). In practice, national accounts compilers, including India's CSO, use a combination of these approaches depending on which is best supported by available data for each sector, exactly as the Sources and Methods document details sector by sector. The other listed pairings (urban/rural/combined, import/export/trade-balance, public/private/household) are not the standard three GDP estimation approaches.

questions.locator: National Accounts Statistics: Sources and Methods 2012, Chapter 1, public sector GVA estimation
questions.source_excerpt: 1.42 Public Sector: The estimates of NVA consists 1.43 of compensation of employees as obtained compensation of employees for the new series for this part have been prepared...
questions.question: For the public sector, the National Accounts Statistics: Sources and Methods, 2012 describes estimating Net Value Added (NVA) primarily using data drawn from which source?
options: Anonymous online surveys of public-sector employees about their perceived productivity
Government budget documents and accounts, from which figures like compensation of employees and operating surplus of public sector enterprises are obtained directly
International Monetary Fund press releases on India's fiscal deficit
Newspaper reports on government spending announcements
questions.explanation: Because public-sector entities (government departments and public sector enterprises) maintain formal, audited accounts and budget documents, the National Accounts methodology can draw directly on this administrative data -- such as compensation of employees, and the analysis of government budgets and accounts of public sector enterprises -- to estimate public-sector value added with a precision that is not achievable for the unorganised private sector (which instead relies on GVAPW-based indirect estimation, as described elsewhere in the same document). This administrative-data-based approach is far more reliable than informal surveys of employee perception, third-party press releases, or newspaper announcements, none of which the Sources and Methods document describes as an input to public-sector GVA estimation.

questions.locator: NQAF-CoCSSO presentation, NQAF Statement 2 ('Managing relationships with data users and data providers')
questions.source_excerpt: NQAF2 Managing relationships with data users and data providers... A Managing the statistical system.
questions.question: In the UN NQAF template's Category A ('Managing the statistical system'), NQAF Statement 2 concerns 'managing relationships with data users and data providers'. Why does a national quality assurance framework treat this relationship management as a system-level quality concern, rather than leaving it purely to individual survey teams?
options: Because data providers (respondents) and data users (policymakers, researchers, the public) are external to any single statistical product, and sustained trust and cooperation with both groups underpins the whole statistical system's ability to collect accurate data and produce statistics that are actually used and trusted -- a systemic condition, not a single survey's concern
Because it only affects the marketing budget of the statistical agency
Because data providers and data users are legally required to be the same set of people under Indian law
Because it has no real bearing on statistical quality and is included only for completeness
questions.explanation: The NQAF places 'managing relationships with data users and data providers' at the system level (Category A) because respondent cooperation (data providers' willingness to give accurate, timely information) and user confidence (data users' trust that the statistics reflect reality and are relevant to their needs) are foundational conditions that affect every statistical product the system produces, not something that can be fixed survey-by-survey. Poor relationship management with providers can degrade response rates and data accuracy across many surveys; poor relationship management with users can mean even accurate statistics go unused or are misunderstood. This is a genuine and central quality concern within the framework, not a marketing afterthought, and there is no legal requirement conflating data providers with data users.

questions.locator: NQAF-CoCSSO presentation, Overall Assessment slide
questions.source_excerpt: Overall Assessment: 108 18 123 1 / Overall Assessment in %: 43.4 7.2 49.4 -
questions.question: Per the NQAF-CoCSSO presentation's overall assessment of the Indian Statistical System against the UN NQAF checklist, roughly what share of quality elements were found to be either fully ('Yes') or partially ('Partially True') met, combined?
options: Roughly 7%, since almost none of the elements were met at all
Roughly 43%, counting only the elements marked fully 'Yes'
Roughly 92-93%, combining the approximately 43% marked fully 'Yes' with the approximately 49% marked 'Partially True'
Exactly 100%, since the assessment found no gaps whatsoever
questions.explanation: The overall assessment reports approximately 43.4% of quality elements marked fully 'Yes', 7.2% marked 'No', and 49.4% marked 'Partially True' (with a negligible remainder 'Not applicable'). Adding the 'Yes' and 'Partially True' shares together gives roughly 92-93% of elements showing at least some degree of compliance, though it is worth noting the assessment's own weighted overall percentage (which counts 'Partially True' at half weight) reports a lower combined figure -- either way, the headline finding is that a large majority of elements show at least partial compliance, but a meaningful share are only partially met, which is exactly why the presentation goes on to list specific structural gaps such as the absence of a legislative framework for the NSO. Options A and B pick out only one component of the breakdown, and option D contradicts the presentation's own explicit finding of gaps.

questions.locator: NQAF-CoCSSO presentation, 'Details on the gap' slide
questions.source_excerpt: Details on the gap in comparison with the NQAF: legislative framework for establishment of NSO; conducting training courses for users on interpreting statistics; involvement of users and data providers in the process for originating, developing and approving statistical standards...
questions.question: The NQAF-CoCSSO presentation lists several specific gaps found when assessing the Indian Statistical System against the NQAF. Which of the following is explicitly listed as one of these gaps?
options: The absence of a legislative framework for the establishment of the National Statistical Office (NSO)
A complete absence of any officially released Consumer Price Index
A complete absence of any Census of India since independence
A ban on publishing any government statistics to the public
questions.explanation: Among the specific gaps the presentation lists relative to the NQAF's expectations are the absence of a dedicated legislative framework establishing the NSO itself, insufficient training courses for users on interpreting statistics, limited involvement of users and data providers in developing statistical standards, incomplete documentation for each production stage, and a lack of identified quality indicators for evaluating production. None of the other options describe real gaps identified in the presentation -- India does have a long-running CPI series and an unbroken Census tradition since 1872 (as the Census manual itself documents), and government statistics are actively published, not banned.

questions.source_excerpt: Supporting documents to the NQAF template: Checklist to review lines of the NQAF... UN guidelines for the template... Glossary of terms as in checklist/ guidelines following SDMX's Metadata Common Vocabulary... questions.question: Besides the 19 quality statements themselves, what supporting documents does the UN NQAF template come with, per the NQAF-CoCSSO presentation?
options: A checklist for self-assessment, UN implementation guidelines, a glossary of terms based on SDMX's Metadata Common Vocabulary, and a mapping of the NQAF against other frameworks like the European Statistics Code of Practice and the IMF's Data Quality Assessment Framework
Only a single-page summary poster and nothing else
A mandatory annual budget allocation formula for every national statistical office
A list of approved software vendors for statistical agencies
questions.explanation: The presentation lists the NQAF template's supporting materials as: a checklist to review and self-assess against the NQAF's lines (marking Yes/No/Partially true/Not applicable), UN guidelines explaining how to interpret and apply each of the 19 quality statements, a glossary of terms aligned with SDMX's Metadata Common Vocabulary (for terminological consistency with other statistical metadata standards), and a mapping showing how the NQAF's statements correspond to other established quality frameworks such as the European Statistics Code of Practice, the IMF's Data Quality Assessment Framework, and others. There is no budget-allocation formula or approved-vendor list among these supporting documents, and the materials are considerably more substantial than a single-page poster.

questions.source_excerpt: National Statistical Systems Training Academy (NSSTA) formerly known as National Academy of Statistical Administration (NASA), established in February, 2009 is a premier institute fostering human resource development in Official Statistics at National and International level.
questions.question: Per the NSSTA Training Calendar 2021-22, what was the National Statistical Systems Training Academy (NSSTA) previously known as, and when was it established?
options: It was previously called the 'National Academy of Statistical Administration (NASA)', established in February 2009
It was previously called the 'Indian Statistical Institute (ISI)', established in 1931
It has always been called NSSTA since India's independence in 1947
It was previously called the 'Central Statistical Office Training Wing', established in 2015
questions.explanation: The Training Calendar's overview states that NSSTA was formerly known as the National Academy of Statistical Administration (NASA), and that it was established in February 2009 as a premier institute for human resource development in Official Statistics at both the national and international level. This is a distinct institution from the much older Indian Statistical Institute (ISI, founded 1931 as a research and teaching institute), and it did not exist under the name NSSTA since 1947 nor was it established in 2015 as a CSO training wing -- both of those are incorrect names/dates not found in the document.

questions.source_excerpt: a. First Phase of MCTP: This phase is for ISS officers of 8-10 years of service... b. Second Phase of MCTP: This phase is for ISS officers of 15-17 years of service... c. Third Phase of MCTP: The third phase of MCTP is for ISS officers of 23-28 years of service.
questions.question: The NSSTA Training Calendar 2021-22 describes the mandatory Mid-Career Training Programme (MCTP) for in-service Indian Statistical Service (ISS) officers as being organized into three phases, tied to years of service. What determines which phase an officer takes?
options: The officer's academic degree (Bachelor's vs Master's) determines the phase, regardless of years of service
The officer's years of service: roughly 8-10 years for the First Phase, 15-17 years for the Second Phase, and 23-28 years for the Third Phase
The officer's home state determines which phase they are assigned to, regardless of seniority
All ISS officers take all three phases in their very first year of service, back to back
questions.explanation: The MCTP is explicitly staged by seniority/years of service: the First Phase targets ISS officers with roughly 8-10 years of service (and includes a Cohort Based Training Programme covering machine learning, big data, and management foundations), the Second Phase targets officers with 15-17 years of service (covering four one-week modules including project management and advanced management), and the Third Phase targets officers with 23-28 years of service (covering leadership, ICT project management, and current economic issues, calibrated for officers nearing the most senior levels of the cadre). This career-stage design ensures training content matches the seniority and likely role of the officer at each point, rather than being tied to academic background, home state, or compressed into a single early-career burst.

options: Module on Foreign Language Translation
Module 1.3: Survey Methodology
Module on Automobile Engineering

questions.explanation: Course 1 of the ISS probationer curriculum, 'Proficiency in Official Statistics', is divided into five modules: 1.1 Official statistics, 1.2 Economics and Financial Statistics, 1.3 Survey Methodology, 1.4 Multivariate Analysis, and 1.5 Monitoring and Evaluation. Survey Methodology (Module 1.3) is explicitly one of these five, reflecting how central survey design and execution is to an ISS officer's core professional competence. Foreign language translation, automobile engineering, and retail marketing are not part of this course's module structure, which is focused squarely on the statistical and analytical skills the ISS cadre needs.
